## **Avian and Bat Post-construction Monitoring at the Pinnacle Wind Farm, Mineral County, West Virginia, 2012**

## **Final Report**

**Cris D. Hein[1] , Alex Prichard[2] , Todd Mabee[2] , and Michael R. Schirmacher[1]**

## **EXECUTIVE SUMMARY**

We initiated a post-construction fatality monitoring study in March 2012, at the Pinnacle Wind Farm (PWF), Mineral County, West Virginia, in accordance with the West Virginia Public Service Commission (WVPSC) and with guidance from the Technical Advisory Committee, which included members from the WVPSC, U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, West Virginia Division of Natural Resources, Edison Mission Energy. The objectives of this study were to determine searcher efficiency and scavenger removal rates, and estimate bird and bat fatality rates at the PWF. An operational mitigation study was conducted at the PWF between 15 July and 30 September 2012, the results of which are discussed in a separate report.

The facility lies within the Appalachian mixed mesophytic forests ecoregion composed of moist broadleaf forests, which cover the plateaus and rolling hills west of the Appalachian Mountains. The project consists of 23 Mitsubishi 2.4-MW turbines, with 95 m rotor diameter and 80 m hub height for a total height of approximately 128 m (from base of tower to highest point of the blade), ), and a manufacturer’s cut-in speed of 3.0 m/s. Turbines are fully “feathered” below the manufacturer’s cut-in speed. In this position, there is no aerodynamic lift from the blades and thus no rotor rotation. At 3.0 m/s the blades are pitched to generate lift and the rotor starts rotation. We conducted weekly fatality searches between 1 March and 30 November 2012. We estimated bat and bird fatality with two different estimators: The Huso estimator (Huso et al. 2012) and a modified version of the Shoenfeld estimator used by Erickson et al. (2004), Kerns and Kerlinger (2004), Kerns et al. (2005).

We found a total of 102 bat carcasses and 2 live bats with no visible injury during standard searches, and 125 incidental carcasses (i.e., not part of standard searches). We recovered carcasses from 5 different species, including eastern red bats ( _Lasiurus borealis_ ), hoary bats ( _Lasiurus cinereus_ ), silver-haired bats ( _Lasionycteris noctivagans_ )-listed as Imperiled (S2) by West Virginia Division of Natural Resources (WVDNR), tri-colored bats ( _Perimyotis subflavus_ ), and big brown bats ( _Eptesicus fuscus_ ). Migratory tree-roosting bats (hoary bats, silver-haired bats, and eastern red bats) comprised nearly 87% (n = 89) of all fatalities found during weekly searches, and big brown bats and tri-colored bats, two species impacted by whitenosed syndrome (WNS), collectively represented 13% of carcasses found. No bats recovered during the study showed signs of WNS. The number of carcasses recovered during weekly searches varied by turbine ranging from 4 at turbine 3 to 24 at turbine 23. The majority of bat fatalities, recovered during weekly searches, occurred in late summer and fall, with 65% (n = 66) carcasses found between July and October. Of the incidental carcasses found, 80% were migratory tree-roosting bats and 18% big brown bats and tri-colored bats. We also found 1 Seminole bat ( _Lasiurus seminolus_ ) and 1 unidentified bat outside of our standard searches. We found no bat carcasses in November.

We used 102 searcher efficiency trial bat carcasses to correct estimates of fatality in this study.  We found 53% (n = 32) and 30% (n = 18) of carcasses from easy and moderate visibility classes, respectively. We used 151 trial bat carcasses to estimate carcass persistence. Average persistence time was estimated to be 0.98 and 1.46 days for easy and moderate visibility classes, respectively. The estimated fatality rate for bats, using the Huso estimator, was 119.21 bats/turbine/year (95% CI: 80.92–184.46), or 49.67 bats/MW/year (95% CI: 33.72–76.86). For

the Shoenfeld estimator, the estimated fatality rate was 96.47 bats/turbine/year (95% CI: 68.62– 146.39), or 40.20 bats/MW/year (95% CI: 28.59–61.0).

We found a total of 25 bird carcasses, of which 14 and 11 were from weekly searches and incidental finds, respectively. Of the 11 different species found during standard searches, only Red-eyed Vireos (n = 3) and Tennessee Warblers (n = 2) were found more than once. The number of carcasses, recovered during weekly searches, varied by turbine ranging from 1 at turbines 6, 10, 12, 17, and 20 to 5 at Turbine 23. Most bird carcasses (n = 9), recovered during weekly searches occurred between March and June. We found 9 different species as incidentals, with Red-eyed Vireo (n = 2) and Mourning Dove (n = 2) carcasses recovered more than once. We found one incidental Nashville Warbler, whose breeding populations are listed as Critically Imperiled (S1B), respectively by the WVDNR. No hawks, eagles or falcons were found during the survey.

We used 91 searcher efficiency trial bird carcasses to correct estimates of fatality for the weekly study.  We found 44% (n = 40) of carcasses. We used 118 trial bird carcasses to estimate carcass persistence. Average persistence time was estimated to be 1.04 days. The estimated fatality rate for birds, using the Huso estimator, was 16.55 birds/turbine (95% CI: 9.50–28.66), or 6.90 birds/MW/year (95% CI: 3.96–11.94). For the Shoenfeld estimator, the estimated fatality rate was 9.58 birds/turbine/year (95% CI: 5.06–17.96), or 3.99 birds/MW/year (95% CI: 2.11– 7.48).

It is unclear at this time as to why the PWF had such high bird and bat fatality rates overall and higher bat fatality during spring and early summer compared to other studies in the region, but landscape or weather conditions may have played a role. The Allegheny Wildlife Management area is within close proximity to the PWF, and likely offers suitable habitat conditions for both resident and migrating bats. During 2012 in the northeastern U.S., winter and spring were relatively mild compared to previous years, presumably causing changes in migratory behavior patterns. When additional 2012 fatality estimates from nearby facilities become available, they may elucidate whether weather conditions influenced fatality patterns at this site or in the region.

## **INTRODUCTION**

With the increasing demand for energy globally, many countries are seeking ways to reduce fossil fuel consumption and generate alternate forms of energy. Recently, wind power has gained prominence among renewable resources driven, in part, by supportive government policies and growing economic competitiveness (Ledec et al. 2011). During the past decade, global wind generating capacity has increased 10-fold, and now exceeds 196,000 MW (World Wind Energy Association 2011, Ledec et al. 2011). In North America, wind-energy is one of the fastest growing forms of renewable energy and has been produced commercially for nearly 4 decades (Pasqualetti et al. 2004, National Research Council 2007). In recent years, the U.S. has been a world leader, second only to China, in wind generating capacity, with 51,630 MW as of 30 September 2012 (AWEA 2012a). Currently, West Virginia ranks 20[th] in the U.S. for installed capacity at 583 MW, with another 310 MW permitted or under construction (AWEA 2012b). Although wind-generated energy reduces carbon and other greenhouse gas emissions associated with climate change, it is not entirely environmentally neutral, because wildlife and habitats can be directly or indirectly impacted by development.

Bat fatalities have been reported at wind facilities since the early 1970’s (Hall and Richards 1972, Dürr and Bach 2004, Kunz et al. 2007, Kuvlesky et al. 2007, Arnett et al. 2008), but have received little attention until 2003, when an estimated 1,400–4,000 fatalities (48 bats/turbine [32 bats/MW]) were reported at the Mountaineer Wind Energy Center, West Virginia (Kerns and Kerlinger 2004). Relatively high fatality rates also have been documented at other facilities along forest ridges across the eastern United States, including Meyersdale, PA (Kerns et al. 2005), Buffalo Mountain, Tennessee (Fielder 2004 and Fiedler et al. 2007), and Cassleman, PA (Arnett et al. 2009), with fatality rates for the region ranging from ~15–53 bats/MW/year (Arnett et al. 2008). Data from the Midwestern U.S. and Canada also suggest moderate to high fatality events occur across a variety of landscapes, including agricultural fields, grassland prairies, and deciduous or coniferous forests (Jain et al. 2011, Barclay et al. 2007, Kunz et al. 2007, Arnett et al. 2008). Concerns regarding the potential cumulative negative effects of anthropogenic activities, including wind energy development, on bat populations persist. Bats have low reproductive rates and require high adult survivorship to avoid population declines (Barclay and Harder 2003). As such, bats are not able to recover quickly from largescale impacts and many species are already known or suspected to be in decline (Pierson 1998, Racey and Entwistle 2003, Winhold and Kurta 2006, Jones et al. 2009, Frick et al. 2010). Because bats provide numerous ecosystem services (e.g., insect suppression), adverse impacts of wind development on local bat populations could disrupt the ecological health and stability of a region (Kunz et al. 2011). Bats are long lived animals with low reproductive rates and populations can take a long time to recover from losses (Barclay and Harder 2003)

Fourteen species of bats are known or suspected to occur in West Virginia (Bat Conservation International 2012). Of these, the Indiana bat ( _Myotis sodalis_ ) is listed by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS) as federally endangered and by the West Virginia Division of Natural Resources (WVDNR) as state critically imperiled (S1), Viginia’s big-eared bat ( _Corynorhinus townsendii virginianus_ ) is federally endangered and state imperiled (S2), the gray bat ( _M. grisescens_ ) as federally endangered, the eastern small-footed bat ( _M. leibii_ ) and Rafinesque’s big-eared ( _C. rafinesquii)_ bat are state critically imperiled, and the silver-haired bat ( _Lasionycteris noctivagans_ ) is state imperiled. Along with the eastern small-footed bat, two other

species, the little brown ( _M. lucifugus_ ) and northern long-eared bat ( _M. septentrionalis_ ) are considered candidates for federal listing. The remaining 6 species, big brown ( _Eptesicus fuscus_ ), tri-colored ( _Perimyotis subflavus_ ), eastern red ( _Lasiurus borealis_ ), Seminole ( _Lasiurus seminolus_ ), hoary ( _Lasiurus cinereus_ ), and evening ( _Nycticeius humeralis_ ) bats are not granted special conservation status at the state or federal level. However, several of these species, collectively known as migratory tree-roosting bats (eastern red bat, hoary bat and silver-haired bat), are of increasing concern with respect to wind development because these species constitute a large majority of fatalities (Arnett et al. 2008).

## **OBJECTIVES**

Although we have studied the impacts of wind energy development on bats for nearly a decade, additional information is needed to understand bat fatality patterns and how bats are interacting with wind turbines. Our goal was to conduct a post-construction fatality monitoring study at the Pinnacle Wind Farm (PWF). Specifically, our objectives were to 1) conduct fatality searches, determine searcher efficiency and scavenger removal rates to adjust number of carcasses found, and estimate bat and bird fatality rates at the site, and 2) evaluate patterns of post-construction bat fatality in relation to wind speed, temperature, rotor speed, and other factors and assess the predictability of fatality based on these factors. During the 2012 field season, we also conducted an operational mitigation study to investigate the effectiveness of raising cut-in speed, from 3 to 5 m/s, for the first half of the night versus all night (see Hein et al. 2013).

## **STUDY AREA**

The PWF is located near the town of Keyser in Mineral County, West Virginia (Fig. 1). The PWF is situated along a 3.5 mile stretch of privately owned land, along a wooded ridge-top on Green Mountain. The PWF consists of 23 Mitsubishi 2.4-MW turbines, with 95 m rotor diameter and 80 m hub height for a total height of approximately 128 m (from base of tower to highest point of the blade), ), and a manufacturer’s cut-in speed of 3.0 m/s. Turbines are fully “feathered” below the manufacturer’s cut-in speed. In this position, there is no aerodynamic lift from the blades and thus no rotor rotation. At 3.0 m/s the blades are pitched to generate lift and the rotor starts rotation. The facility lies within the Appalachian mixed mesophytic forests ecoregion composed of moist broadleaf forests, which cover the plateaus and rolling hills west of the Appalachian Mountains (Brown and Brown 1972, Strausbaugh and Core 1978).  The elevation of the project area varies from 766 to 869 m above mean sea level.

## **METHODS**

_**Delineation of Carcass Search Plots and Habitat Mapping.**_ We initiated a postconstruction fatality monitoring study following protocols outlined in the Pinnacle Wind, LLC Avian and Bat Protection Plan. We conducted weekly searches at 11 turbines from 1 March–30 November 2012. We used a random numbers table to randomly select 11 of the available 23 turbines to be searched (Randomly selected turbines: 3, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 15, 17, 18, 20, and 23). This process reduces potential bias in the turbine selection and prevents artificially inflating or deflating fatality estimates. We attempted to delineate a rectangular plot 126 m east-west by 120 m northsouth (15,120 m[2] total area) centered on each turbine sampled; this area represents the maximum possible search area for this study (see Fig. 2 for an example). We set transects 6 m apart within

each plot and observers searched 3 m on each side of the transect line. We considered contiguous forest cover and areas unsafe to search as unsearchable habitat (e.g. steep terrain) and eliminated them from our search plots. Because the area cleared of forest varied by search plot, actual searchable area differed among turbines (see Appendix 1). We used a Trimble GeoXT (Trimble Navigation Limited, Sunnyvale, CA) global positioning system (GPS) to map the actual area searched at each turbine (Appendix 1). The density weighted area searched was used to standardize results and adjust fatality estimates (see below). We mapped the habitat visibility classes within each plot with a GPS unit.

_**Fatality Searches**_ **.** We conducted a "clean-out" search, in conjunction with our first search day, of each plot to remove carcasses present prior to 1 March. We abandoned searches only when heavy rain, lightning, snow, or turbine maintenance created a safety hazard, as determined by the lead field biologist (M. R. Schirmacher); searches were resumed that day if conditions permitted. Searches commenced within 15 minutes of sunrise, and we attempted to search all turbines within 8 hours after sunrise. We recorded date, start time, end time, turbine number, weather, and observer for each search. When a dead bat or bird was found, the searcher placed a rock pile near the carcass, noted the time, contacted the crew leader, and continued the search. In most cases the crew leader, but on rare events the searcher after searching the entire plot, recorded information on a fatality data sheet, including date, species, sex and age (when possible), observer name, turbine number, perpendicular distance from the transect line to the carcass, distance from turbine, azimuth from turbine, habitat surrounding carcass, condition of carcass (entire, partial, scavenged), and estimated time of death (e.g., <1 day, 2 days) based on condition of the carcass (e.g., eyes, smell, insects), in addition photographs were taken for each carcass. We visually examined each bat carcasses for obvious signs of white-nose syndrome using the Reichard scoring index (Reichard and Kunz 2009). The lead field biologist (M. R. Schirmacher, a USFWS Indiana bat qualified surveyor) confirmed all species identifications each day. We used rubber gloves to handle all carcasses to reduce possible human scent bias for carcasses later used in scavenger removal trials. We placed each carcass in a labeled plastic bag and stored them in a secured and dedicated freezer at the Operations and Maintenance office building. We obtained a USFWS Special Purpose Utility Permit for Migratory Bird Mortality Monitoring (MB74673A-0) and a Scientific Collecting Permit (No. 2012.077) from the West Virginia Division of Natural Resources to handle bird and bat carcasses.

Incidental fatalities were defined as those found outside of the search plot, found in the search plot but determined killed before the study was initiated (e.g., carcasses missed during “clean-out”), or found at an unsearched turbine.  Carcasses found by non-search personnel (e.g., crew leaders, wind technicians) were left until found during a scheduled search, but were considered incidentals if scavenged or not found within 20 days. Incidental fatalities were reported to the crew leader and recorded, but were not included in analysis of fatality estimates. Similar to carcasses found during standard searches, we placed each incidental carcass is a labeled plastic bag and stored them in a secured and dedicated freezer at the Operations and Maintenance office building.

_**Field Bias Trials.**_ We quantified searcher efficiency and removal of carcasses by scavengers at all sampled turbines to adjust the estimate of total bird and bat fatalities. We conducted bias trials throughout the entire study period and at all sampled turbines, and searchers were never aware which turbines were used or the number of carcasses placed beneath those turbines during trials. In most cases, we used freshly killed (i.e., carcasses determined to have

been killed the previous night) for our bias trial, but we did use frozen carcasses when necessary, particularly for bird trials. Additional bird carcasses were provided by the USFWS. We used a list of random turbine numbers, and random azimuths and distances (m) from turbines for placement of each carcass used in bias trials. We also used carcasses of actual fatalities if found by non-search personnel, who left the carcass in place, until found during a scheduled search.

Data recorded for each trial carcass prior to placement included date and time of placement, species, turbine number, distance and direction from turbine, and visibility class surrounding the carcass.  We attempted to distribute trial carcasses equally among the different visibility classes throughout the study period. We attempted to avoid “over-seeding” any one turbine with carcasses at any one time at a given turbine. Each trial carcass was left in place and checked by the lead field biologist or crew leader; who were not involved with daily searches. Thus, trial carcasses were available to be found by searchers on consecutive searches during weekly searches unless removed by a scavenger. We recorded the day and time that each bat or bird was found by a searcher, at which time the carcass was marked with a rock pile and remained in the scavenger removal trial. If, however, a carcass was removed by a scavenger before detection by a searcher (i.e., carcass not present before search was conducted) it was removed from the searcher efficiency trial and used only in the carcass removal data set. Carcasses were left in place until removed by a scavenger or at the end of the twenty day trial. Carcass condition was recorded daily up to 20 days, as present and observable (1) or missing or no longer observable (0).

## **Statistical Methods**

_**Carcass Persistence**_ .  Estimates of the probability that a bat or bird carcass was not removed in the interval between searches were used to adjust carcass counts for removal bias. Removal was defined as a carcass not present within the searchable plot (i.e., removed by scavenging, wind or water) or lasted until the end of the trial (e.g., 20 days). The length of time a carcass remains on the study area before it is removed can be modeled as an exponential, weibull, loglogistic or lognormal distributed random variable. For both birds and bats (separately), we fit carcass persistence time data to each of these failure time models with and without visibility class as a covariate and used Akaike’s Information Criterion (AICc)model selection in Fatality Estimator software (Huso et al. 2012) to determine the best model (Burnham and Anderson 2002). Because there were inadequate sample sizes to compare different carcasses sized for birds, carcass size was not considered a variable. There also were inadequate sample sizes to compare all visibility classes, therefore the moderate and difficult classes were combined into a moderate category. Hence, we compared eight models for carcass persistence (intercept only and visibility for four different distributions [weibull, exponential, loglogistic, and lognormal]).

_**Searcher Efficiency.**_ Estimates of the probability that a carcass will be seen by an observer during a search were used to adjust carcass counts for observer bias. The failure of an observer to detect a carcass on the search plot may be due to its size, color, or time since death, as well as conditions in its immediate vicinity (e.g., vegetation density, shade). In most fatality monitoring efforts, because we cannot measure time since death, it is assumed that a carcass’s “observability” is constant over the period of the search interval, although it likely is not (Warren Hicks et al. 2012).  In this study, searches were conducted weekly and carcass persistence times

were short, providing limited opportunity for a searcher to detect a carcass that was missed on a previous search. After accounting for carcasses removed before a searcher had the chance of observing them, data from bat and bird searcher efficiency trials were fit separately to a logistic regression model using the Fatality Estimator (Huso et al. 2012). We modeled searcher efficiency for bats that included visibility class as a covariate and assessed model fit using AICc (Burnham and Anderson 2002). Due to the inadequate sample sizes for birds, we were unable to compare different carcasses sizes for birds. There also were inadequate sample sizes to compare all visibility classes, therefore the moderate and difficult classes were combined into a moderate category. Hence, we compared two models for searcher efficiency (intercept only and visibility).

_**Density of carcasses and proportion of area surveyed.**_ The actual area surveyed within a plot varies among turbines and from the delineated theoretical maximum search plot. Density of carcasses is known to diminish with increasing distance from the turbine (e.g., Kerns et al. 2005). A simple adjustment to fatality based on area surveyed would likely lead to over estimates, because unsearched areas tend to be farthest from turbines. The size and configuration of the area searched can greatly affect the proportion of actual fatality represented in the searched area. To accurately estimate the fraction of carcasses landing in the sampled areas, we calculated the total area in each visibility category within each 2 m band from the base of each turbine. We also calculated the number of carcasses (either bird or bat) that were found in each 2 m distance band and visibility class. We used a Poisson regression to model the number of birds or bats that were found by distance from turbine and visibility class. Distance was treated as a continuous independent variable and visibility class was treated as a categorical independent variable. We used Akaike’s Information Criterion for small samples (AICc) selection to select between linear and a quadratic logistic models (Burnham and Anderson 2002). Visibility was included in the models as an adjustment for differences in number of carcasses found due to searcher efficiency. The methods described follow those of Huso and Dalthorp (in press). The best model was used to predict the number of fatalities that would have been found in the entire search area if the entire area was in the easy visibility class. We used as our density-weighted proportion, the number of fatalities, for birds and bats, predicted to fall in the searchable area divided by the total number predicted in the entire plot. The process was implemented twice, modeling bat and small birds separately.

_**Fatality estimates.**_ We used two methods to estimate fatality rates for birds and bats. We estimated fatality using the Fatality Estimator software (Huso et al. 2012) and using the equations of Erickson et al. (2004), which were modified from Shoenfeld (2004), hereafter the Shoefeld estimator. Differences in fatality estimates between the two estimators are largest when search intervals are much shorter than average persistence time.  Huso’s estimator assumes that a carcass missed on an initial search will not be found in subsequent searches, leading to an overestimate of fatality when search intervals are short and all found carcasses are used in the estimator regardless of the amount of time elapsed since their death.  Schoenfeld’s assumes that any carcass missed on an initial search will have the same probability of discovery on a subsequent search, leading to an underestimate of fatality when search intervals are short. Recent unpublished work by Wolpert et al. (2012) indicates that searcher efficiency probably diminishes with time so that the actual process lies somewhere between the two assumptions.

Because Huso’s estimator assumes all carcasses are fresh (in the case of weekly searches, ‘fresh’ equals carcasses from 1-7 days old, for daily searches, ‘fresh’ equals carcasses one day old), the bias in her methods can be removed by using only fresh carcasses in the fatality

_**Model Analysis.**_ To assess the relationship between fatality and various turbine and weather variables, we compiled data, collected by 11 turbines sampled during weekly searches. For each turbine-night, we calculated the number of ‘fresh’ (determined to have occurred the previous night) bat fatalities found the next morning and the calculated the distance-weighted

proportion of searchable area for each turbine. The weather variables calculated included: the proportion of the night with rotations per minute (RPM) <1; the proportion of the night with RPM’s >9; the proportion of the night with wind speeds <3 m/s; the proportion of the night with wind speeds <5 m/s; the proportion of the night with wind speeds between 3 and 5 m/s; the proportion of the night with temperatures >9.5° C; the proportion of the night with temperatures >8° C; the difference between the minimum and maximum pressure (mbar) 12 hr prior to sunset; the difference between the minimum and maximum pressure (mbar) 6 hr prior to sunset; the mean Cosine of wind direction during the night; the mean Sine of wind direction during the night; the proportion of the night with temperatures >9.5° C for the night prior to the night searched; and the proportion of the night with wind speeds >5 m/s for the night prior to the night searched.

We tested 40 different predetermined candidate models to determine the best variables to describe the occurrence of bat fatalities among turbines. Model selection was conducted using Information Theoretic approach. For each parameter, we calculated the model-averaged parameter estimate by weighting estimates by the Akaike’s weight (ωi; Burnham and Anderson 2002). All models were run as Poisson regression models with the number of fatalities at each turbine for each night as the response variable (n = 446). The distance weighted proportion of the area searched (natural log transformed) was included as an offset term to account for different search areas among different turbines. There was no evidence of overdispersion in the models.

The models tested included an intercept only model, turbine only model, 13 models with turbine and 1 weather variable, and 5 models with turbine and two weather variables. These 20 models were run with and without date of search in the models for a total of 40 models. The date of search was included as a cubic term with the date of the first search set to zero to facilitate parameter interpretation. The cubic form of date was compared to models with a linear or cubic form and found to have a lower AICc value.

## **RESULTS**

_**Fatality Searches**_ **.** We were able to search turbines 100% of the time during weekly searches. Due to the differences among turbine plot sizes, average search time varied across the site ranging from 39 minutes for Turbine 15 to 58 minutes for Turbine 18 (Table 2). There also was variation in search times within each turbine plot because of different searchers or weather conditions.

_**Carcass Persistence**_ .  We used 151 trial bat carcasses to estimate carcass persistence for weekly turbines. The most parsimonious model for carcass persistence for bats was the lognormal distribution (Table 3). Average persistence time was estimated to be 0.98 and 1.46 days for easy and moderate visibility classes, respectively (Table 4). We used 118 trial bird carcasses to estimate carcass persistence. For birds, the most parsimonious model was the loglogistic distribution. Average persistence time was estimated to be 1.04 days.

_**Searcher Efficiency.**_ We used 122 searcher efficiency trial bat carcasses (61 trials each in easy and moderate visibility classes). We found 52% (n = 32) and 30% (n = 18) of carcasses from easy and moderate visibility classes, respectively (Table 5). The most parsimonious model for searcher efficiency included the visibility variable (2 classes) for bats (Table 6). We used 91 searcher efficiency trial bird carcasses and found 44% (n = 40) during the trials for all visibility and size classes combined. _**Bat Fatality.**_ We found a total of 102 bat carcasses and 2 live bats, with no visible injury, during standard searches, and 125 incidental carcasses (i.e., found outside of standard searches; Table 8). We recovered carcasses from 5 different species, including eastern red bats, hoary bats, silver-haired bats-listed, tri-colored bats, and big brown bats. Migratory tree-roosting bats (i.e., hoary bats, silver-haired bats, and eastern red bats) comprised 87% (n = 89) of all fatalities found during weekly searches, and tri-colored and big brown bats, two species affected by white-nose syndrome (WNS), collectively represented 13% (n = 13) of carcasses recovered. The total number of carcasses recovered during weekly searches varied by turbine ranging from 4 at turbine 3 to 24 at turbine 23 (Table 9). The majority of bat fatalities, recovered during weekly searches, occurred in late summer and fall, with 65% (n = 66) carcasses found between July and October (Table 10, Fig. 3). Of the incidental carcasses found, 48 were eastern red bats, 41 hoary bats, 13 tri-colored bats, 11 silver-haired bats, and 10 big brown bats. We found 1 Seminole bat

and 1 unidentifiable bat as incidentals. We found no bat carcasses in November. No bats recovered during the study showed signs of WNS.

The estimated fatality rate for bats, using the Huso estimator, was 119.21 bats/turbine/year (95% CI: 80.92–184.46), or 49.67 bats/MW/year (95% CI: 33.72–76.86; Table 11). For the Shoenfeld estimator, the estimated fatality rate was 96.47 bats/turbine/year (95% CI: 68.62–146.39), or 40.20 bats/MW/year (95% CI: 28.59–61.0). Eastern red bats had the highest fatality rate among the different species, followed by hoary bats and silver-haired bats (Table 12).

_**Model Analysis.**_ There were a total of 62 fatalities that were determined to have occurred the previous night during 446 turbine-nights of searches. There were 396 turbine-nights with zero fresh fatalities detected, 41 turbine-nights with 1 fresh fatality, 6 turbine-nights with 2 fresh fatalities, and 3 turbine-nights with 3 fresh fatalities. The average estimated DWP that was searchable was 60.5 indicating that approximately 103 fresh fatalities could potentially have been found if all the area was searchable.

The most parsimonious model in our candidate model set included the variables date (as a cubic term), turbine, and the proportion of wind speeds between 3–5 m/s during the night (Table 15). This model had high support as the best model (ωi = 0.741), given the data and candidate set of models. The second best model was similar, with the proportion of wind <5 m/s instead of wind between 3–5 m/s. This second model had an AICc value 3.941 times higher (ωi = 0.105), indicating little support. Models without a date term had no support suggesting that there was a seasonal pattern in bat fatalities that could not be explained by the available weather data. When only models without date were considered, however, the model with wind speed 3–5 m/s was still the best model (ωi = 0.765) suggesting that the effect of this variable was still apparent without accounting for differences by date.

In the best model, the number of fatalities increased over the study until August 23[rd ] and then declined after that date. The fatality rate increased with the proportion of wind speeds between 3–5 m/s (Table 16; Figure 5). Although not in the best model, several other weather variables appeared to be significantly related to the fatality rate. The fatality rate increased when wind speed was <5 m/s ( _P_ = 0.001), and declined with higher values of Cosine of wind direction ( _P_ = 0.034).

We only recovered 14 bird carcasses during weekly searches. Of those, only 5 were determined to be fresh. Thus, we were unable to model bird fatalities with turbine and weather data.

## **DISCUSSION**

At the Pinnacle Wind Farm (PWF), the fatality estimate, based on weekly searches for bats, using the Shoenfeld estimator (which is more comparable among studies because of its widespread use) was approximately 4 times higher than the average fatality estimate (24.6 bats/turbine, range 6.8–42.7) reported in the Pennsylvania Game Commission’s Voluntary Cooperative Agreement annual report from 2007–2009 (PGC 2011).  Similarly, the PWF had the highest bat fatality rate compared to Arnett et al. (2008), which reported mean fatality rates for six studies in the eastern U.S. The bat fatality estimate at the PWF, also was higher than those reported from the Mount Storm Wind Energy Facility, West Virginia from 2008–2011 (Efroymson et al. 2012). It is unclear at this time as to why the PWF had such high fatality rates overall, and higher fatality during spring and early summer compared to other studies, but landscape or weather conditions may have played a role. The Allegheny Wildlife Management area is within close proximity to the PWF, and likely offers suitable habitat conditions for both resident and migrating bats. During 2012 in the northeastern U.S., winter and spring were relatively mild compared to previous years, presumably causing changes in migratory behavior

patterns. When results from nearby facilities with estimates for 2012 become available, they may elucidate whether weather conditions played a role in regionally high fatality numbers.

We found bat fatalities were heavily skewed toward migratory tree-roosting bats, a common pattern observed in North America (Arnett et al. 2008, Baerwald and Barclay 2009).  In West Virginia, during the seven study periods, between fall 2008 and fall 2011, at the Mount Storm Wind Energy Facility, 56–92% of fatalities were composed of migratory tree-roosting bats (Efroymson et al. 2012). Although several attraction hypotheses (e.g., roost, landscape, acoustic, or visual) have been proposed, interactions between bats and wind turbines are poorly understood (Arnett 2005, Barclay et al. 2007, Cryan and Brown 2007, Kunz et al. 2007). Resolution of these different hypotheses requires additional data on the flight behavior of bats.

We found relatively few fatalities of tri-colored bats and no carcasses of the genus _Myotis_ (e.g., little brown bat, Indiana bat, northern long-eared bat, eastern small-footed bat) were recovered during our study. In the eastern U.S., tri-colored bat and myotis fatalities can each exceed 25% of all carcasses recovered. Although none of the bats recovered during this study exhibited signs of WNS, the small percentage of these species found at the PWF may be attributed to the disease, which has devastated bat populations in the region (Turner et al. 2011). In Pennsylvania, Arnett et al. (2010) reported a dramatic decline in the occurrence of these bats between 2009 (pre-WNS in the state) and 2010 (post-WNS), with tri-colored bat fatalities falling from 24% to 10%, and little brown bat fatalities falling from 24% to 4% between years. Although it is unclear how bat populations are affected by the combination of WNS and wind energy fatalities, these combination of factors may contribute to widespread population declines for these species and should receive future consideration.

The majority of fatalities at the PWF occurred between July and October, which is consistent with Arnett et al. (2008, 2010) and PGC (2011). At the Casselman Wind Energy Project, 84% and 81.4% of fatalities occurred between 15 July and 15 October 2008 and 2009, respectively (Arnett et al. 2009, Arnett unpublished data).  At Buffalo Mountain Wind Facility, TN, 71.0, 81.8, 95.3 and 83.0% of fatalities occurred from 15 July–30 September 2001–2003 and 2005, respectively (Fiedler 2004, Fiedler et al. 2007).  This pattern also coincides with records of migrating bats striking other anthropogenic structures and their arrival at migration stopovers (Cryan and Brown 2007). Yet, migration alone cannot explain higher fatality rates in the fall, because no such occurrence is observed during spring migration. Many of the species affected by wind turbines engage in mating activity during peak periods of fatality (Cryan 2008). Increased activity associated with finding mates may increase bat/turbine interactions (Cryan and Barclay 2009).

The proportion of the night wind speeds were between 3 and 5 m/s and <5 m/s related to higher fatality rates at the PWF. Bat activity tends to decrease with increasing wind speeds, particularly at speeds >6 m/s (Reynolds 2006, Horn et al. 2008). This trend appears consistent among wind energy facilities (Arnett et al. 2008), leading hypotheses that shutting down turbines during low wind nights during periods of peak activity could reduce bat fatalities (Kunz et al. 2007, Arnett et al. 2008). In the region, Arnett el al (2011) documented a 44–93% reduction in fatalities that resulted from raising the turbine cut-in speed from 3.5 m/s to 5.0 and 6.5 m/s. Young et al. (2011) demonstrated approximately 72% and 50% reduction in fatality when turbine blades were feathered below 4 m/s for the first 5 hours past sunset, and the 5 hours preceding sunrise, respectively. Wind direction also related to fatality, such that fatalities decreased with

higher values of the Cosine of wind direction (i.e., winds from the north). Contrary to other studies (Kerns et al. 2005, Reynolds 2006, Arnett et al. 2010), we found no evidence that temperature or changes in air pressure prior to nightly activity influenced bat fatality.

Our estimate for bird fatality, using the Shoenfeld estimator, based on weekly searches, was 9.58 birds/turbine. This is approximates 2.5 times higher than the mean estimate, but within the range for 7 facilities in Pennsylvania (mean 3.9, range 1.7–9.8; PGC 2011). At the Mount Storm Wind Energy Facility, Efroymson et al. (2012) reported estimates of bird fatality ranging from 0.7–7.79 birds/turbine. While the significance of these fatalities is unknown, avian fatalities appear to generally be low in this region, although cumulative impacts may become more pronounced as wind energy development expands. We observed no pattern in bird fatalities across the study period. The majority of bird fatalities were passerines, particularly Red-eyed Vireos. No hawks, eagles or falcons were found during the survey. This pattern is common across studies in the eastern U.S. (PGC 2011, Efroymson et al. 2012).

The two fatality estimators provided different, albeit overlapping, fatality estimates for bats, with the Huso estimator higher than the Shoenfeld estimator. Possible reasons for this difference include their treatment of carcass bleed-through and the distribution used to estimate carcass persistence. Huso et al. (2012) assumes that carcasses have a fixed probability of being found on the first search after a fatality event and does not account for carcasses missed during the first search but found on subsequent searches (i.e., bleed-through). Including carcasses that were already missed once would artificially inflate fatality estimates, since those carcasses are already accounted for by applying the searcher efficiency adjustment. Erickson et al. (2004) allows for 100% bleed-through, carcasses that remain on the plot have a constant probability of being found each search. However, recent studies have shown that searcher efficiency declines with age of the carcass (Warren-Hicks et al. 2012), suggesting a potential negative bias in these calculations. Moreover, the Shoenfeld estimator uses an exponential distribution to model carcass persistence while the Huso estimator allows the user to select the best distribution from 4 possible choices. In these studies, the exponential distribution was consistently the distribution with the poorest fit.

Fatality studies should be designed so that the average carcass persistence time is longer than the search interval (Strickland et al. 2011). However, it is difficult to predict removal rates prior to the initiation of a study. When removal time is less than the search interval, it is recommended to use either the Shoenfeld or Huso estimator, and it is preferable to use more than one estimator (Strickland et al. 2011). Carcass persistence at the PWF was among the shortest reported (Arnett et al. 2008), although the Mountaineer Wind Energy Facility, West Virginia had similar removal rates for the second year of the study. At Mount Storm, the persistence rate dropped over the 3 year study from 5.25 days to 2.58 days (Young et al. 2009, 2011). It is not uncommon for removal rates to increase among years at a site as local scavengers learn of a relatively available food source. The low carcass persistence rate in conjunction with a seven day search interval likely caused higher variation in the confidence interval estimated for the point estimate of fatality. Based on the removal rate at the PWF, future monitoring should be done using daily searches. Searching turbines daily also would allow for more ‘fresh’ carcasses to be recovered and related to the previous night’s weather conditions, possibly aiding in determining fatality patterns related to weather variables (e.g., wind speed and temperature).
